parts.label: a
parts.ask: The first 3 terms of a geometric sequence are \(3^{4k-5}\), \(9^{7-2k}\), \(3^{2(k-1)}\). Using algebra, prove that \(k = \tfrac{5}{2}\).
parts.method: Equal ratios, then a common base of 3

steps.why: In a geometric sequence each term is the one before times \(r\), so the two ratios are equal.
Write 9 as \(3^2\) so every term has the same base. Power of a power: multiply the indices.
Multiplying powers of the same base: add the indices.
Same base on both sides, so the indices are equal.

slips: Dividing the indices instead of subtracting them when dividing powers, which led to a quadratic in \(k\).
Subtracting indices of \(9^{\ldots}\) and \(3^{\ldots}\) without first changing to the same base.
Substituting \(k = \tfrac{5}{2}\) to check the sequence is geometric. That verifies, it doesn't prove, and scored at most 1 mark.
Stopping at \(k = \tfrac{35}{14}\): simplify to the given form.

parts.label: b
parts.ask: Hence find the sum to infinity of the sequence.

steps.why: \(|r| < 1\), so the sum to infinity exists.

slips: Using \(r = 3\), the ratio upside down, or \(r = \tfrac{5}{2}\). Neither has \(|r| < 1\), which should have been a warning sign.
